This study proposes a continuous modeling approach for manipulative participation and examines its integration with stance analysis. Using online discourse on the 2024 Street Animal Law in Türkiye as a case study, we collected a dataset comprising 7,320,574 tweets from 537,994 users. From this corpus, 301 users were selected through a high-information sampling strategy and manually annotated by domain experts using a 10-criterion rubric that yields user-level continuous manipulative participation scores. Evaluation under a unified user-level cross-validation protocol showed that the proposed framework accurately estimates both manipulative participation and user stance, with gradient boosting methods providing the best manipulative participation estimates and BERTurk achieving the highest stance classification performance. External validation on an independently annotated user set demonstrated good generalization performance. The findings support modeling manipulative participation as a continuous construct rather than a binary label, providing a more informative basis for computational analyses of the relationship between manipulative participation and stance in online political discourse.
comment: Submitted to Journal of Computational Social Science

title: Recursive Pricing and Incumbent Subtree Column Generation for Solving Optimal Classification Trees
summary: Solving optimal classification tree (OCT) problems is computationally challenging because branching, routing, and leaf-assignment decisions must be optimized jointly. We develop an incumbent subtree column generation algorithm (ISCG-OCT) that exploits the recursive structure of classification trees. We first introduce a mixed set-packing and set-partitioning formulation (MSSF). We then construct a restricted master problem whose columns represent feasible subtree patterns. Unlike conventional dual-based column generation, our incumbent-centered pricing evaluates objective improvements relative to the current solution. We establish a recursive decomposition in which fixing a branching decision separates the remaining pricing problem into independent subtree subproblems, enabling exact dynamic programming. We also develop threshold-based variants that trade optimality guarantees for computational efficiency. Computational experiments on 27 benchmark datasets demonstrate competitive training and testing accuracy and substantial reductions in solution time on many instances. When initialized with a CART solution, ISCG-OCT can certify global optimality faster than warm-started mixed-integer programming solvers on selected instances. These results demonstrate how recursive pricing and structured subtree optimization can improve the computational efficiency of exact classification tree methods.

title: Qubit-to-Motion: Traceable Action Provenance in Hybrid QRL for Robotic Bin-Packing Sequencing
summary: Hybrid quantum reinforcement learning has been explored for robotic decision-making, but evaluations often emphasize task success, return, or convergence, leaving unresolved whether quantum circuit outputs influence constrained actions and remain traceable through robot execution. We present \texttt{Qubit-to-Motion}, an evidence-centered framework for support-constrained sequencing and simulated robotic placement. Four Pauli-$Z$ readouts provide the sole learned input to the actor and critic, while a support mask enforces admissible object selection. Each decision is recorded and linked via step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints to a sealed route, deterministic Cartesian and inverse-kinematics waypoints, prescribed joint motion, and MuJoCo contact replay. A frozen checkpoint is evaluated across five deterministic 30-object scene variants. All 150 placements satisfy support, containment, and settling criteria. A fixed-state zero-readout intervention changes $90.0\pm0.0\%$ of decisions, demonstrating dependence on the joint circuit representation. Mean macro travel is $34.537\pm0.206$~m, inference requires $8.60\pm1.27$~ms per route, and replay achieves $8.764\pm0.220~\mu$m mean final position error with 0.356~mm maximum interpenetration. These results establish reproducible decision-to-contact traceability. The implementation is available at \href{this https URL}{\textcolor{linkpink}{the anonymous repository}}.

title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
summary: A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. Two studies with plans fixed before data collection, across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters, compare the next action and subsequent task completion, with exact deterministic reruns. A new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure observed in Llama models when that exchange is removed. It is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons, but is not best for every model. We implement this form as an opt-in recovery layer within a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent. On ToolMaze, it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models; Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, scored by final-state agreement, shows no measurable gain. A client given the exact fault kind performs better still. The findings support delivery as a distinct factor in recovery, not an engine-exclusive solution or a universal retry policy.

title: NightSteps: A Night-Time Dataset and Benchmark for Pedestrian Crossing Intention Prediction
summary: Autonomous vehicles use pedestrian crossing intention prediction (PCIP) to participate safely in traffic. Existing models are largely trained under favourable daytime conditions with sufficient daylight. Little is known about the robustness of these models under night-time and low-light conditions, due to the lack of datasets containing night-time footage. This paper investigates how a dataset, named NightSteps, can be constructed and evaluated as a baseline benchmark. The dataset is based on nighttime dashcam footage collected from six different cities around the world, capturing a wide variety of road conditions. The dataset consists of dashcam-recorded point-of-view footage, raw data of pedestrians' locations with corresponding 'track ids' and ground-truth labels containing accurate information about pedestrian crossing behaviour, resulting in a diverse dataset. Gemini, ChatGPT, and human assessment are used to demonstrate the usability of the dataset by predicting crossings in clips from the dataset and comparing the results with the initial ground-truth labels. These results show that human input achieves an accuracy of 88.17% and an F1-score of 80.21%. Predictions from Gemini and ChatGPT perform lower, with accuracies of 60% and 79.13% respectively, and F1-scores of 42.50% and 63.64%. The evaluation demonstrates that the NightSteps dataset can be used for future model evaluation to test the performance of PCIP, with the aim of improving road safety at night.

title: FastGRT: Accelerating Training of 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing
summary: Ray Tracing enables rendering capabilities that are difficult to achieve with rasterization-based approaches such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). However, the training cost of Gaussian-based ray tracing (GRT) is much higher than that of 3DGS. In this paper, we study how ray tracing using Gaussians executes on GPUs and show that a considerable fraction of the training cost arises from how the computation is organized. We develop FastGRT, which decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses work done in the forward pass for the backward pass. FastGRT further incorporates optimizations such as fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to tackle other major bottlenecks in the training pipeline. We implement FastGRT in Vulkan. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first Vulkan-based GRT implementation that supports both training and rendering. Compared to 3DGRT, FastGRT improves training time by 1.9$\times$ to 4.97$\times$, while preserving the original rendering formulation. Our code is open source.

title: FinCutBench: A Continually Updated Benchmark for Measuring the Temporal Boundaries of LLM Financial Knowledge
summary: In financial backtesting and other point-in-time tasks, external inputs can be restricted by date, but model parameters may retain financial facts disclosed later, introducing parametric look-ahead bias. We introduce FinCutBench, a continually updated monthly financial knowledge benchmark for measuring how far a fixed model's financial knowledge extends over calendar time. The current dataset contains 9,000 Chinese and English four-option multiple-choice questions from January 2023 to September 2026, covering Chinese and U.S. markets and four categories of financial information. We construct monthly knowledge profiles using the approximate months in which the tested facts became public. After a profile passes the decline test and knot checks, we define the FinCut Boundary as the first month when the fitted profile reaches its lower level, and report the stability of the estimated date under resampling. Boundary dates and localization precision vary across models. Using the independently measured Transition Start and Boundary as fixed references for downstream sample grouping, we find clear relative declines after the Boundary in U.S. asset ranking and earnings recall for some models, while Chinese-market ranking estimates vary across models and all eight disclosure-period-paired forecast-error comparisons have unadjusted $p$ values above 0.10. The FinCut Boundary thus provides an empirical reference for the temporal scope of parametric knowledge in point-in-time financial evaluation, supporting evaluation-window selection and result interpretation.

title: LAION-Audio-XL: A Web-Scale Corpus and Scaling Studies for Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining
summary: Recent progress on contrastive audio-language models can be attributed mainly to the scale and quality of their training data. Larger training datasets expose models to a broader range of sounds and corresponding audio captions. To exploit this, we collect 1.48 billion audio samples from academic datasets, internet datasets, web collections, Common Crawl, and YouTube, and process them with a multi-stage curation pipeline. Furthermore, we generate short and long captions for samples in our corpus that lack them. We use our dataset to study the scaling behavior of contrastive audio-language models based on the NaFlex architecture for the audio encoder. Our experiments identify trade-offs between model size and training data for a given compute budget. Moreover, our resulting models, CLAP2, outperform prior audio-text models of comparable size on the MAEB and HEAR benchmarks. We release our dataset, captions, model checkpoints, and code.

title: Out of Parameters, Saved by Syntax: UD-PrMPT for Parser Augmented Low Resource Machine Translation
summary: Recent work advancing machine translation quality using LLMs for very low resource languages has relied on the injection of lexicon-based prompt components to expose vocabulary to models. However, these approaches run into a ceiling when models must guess sentence meaning purely from plausible combinations of possible word senses mapped to strings. In this paper we test UD-PrMPT, an approach using syntactic analyses in the Universal Dependencies formalism as prompt components to improve MT in five diverse low resource languages: Beja, Chintang, Chukchi, Coptic, and Xibe. Our results show additive improvements which stack on top of the lexicon based approach which are stronger for higher quality manual analyses but consistent for predicted parses as well.

title: Perturbing Inputs Improves Pretraining Distillation
summary: Knowledge distillation trains a student language model to match a teacher's predictions on the training text. We ask whether learning the teacher's behavior beyond the training text can further improve the student. We investigate this using three input perturbations: additive token noise, blending two documents, and blending neighboring tokens. Specifically, for an early part of pretraining we perturb the inputs and train the student to match the teacher on them, and we spend the rest of the same token budget on ordinary distillation. When pretraining from scratch, the best method improves on standard distillation at both scales we tried, by 0.025 nats at 135M parameters and by 0.020 nats at 0.5B (mean of three seeds). At 135M this is 1.45 times the gain that distillation itself provides over next-token training. We also observe promising downstream transfer: at 0.5B, the best variant improves average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks. It also retains its validation-loss advantage after low-bit weight quantization. We also test a data-limited setting in which training data must be reused, and find that the gains persist. Finally, ablations suggest that, for additive noise, perturbing the teacher's inputs contributes most of the gain, while perturbing only the student's inputs yields much less.

title: Kinora: A Versioned Workflow for Text-to-Motion Generation, Robot Retargeting, and Interactive Validation
summary: Motion generation tools produce candidate trajectories, but interactive robot authoring also requires recoverable execution, traceable edits, explicit geometry, and model-specific validation. We present Kinora, a system that connects text-to-motion generation, a motion library, local agent tools, robot retargeting, and trajectory refinement through versioned artifacts. The current release uses an independently specified 52-joint authoring rig and procedural skeleton previews, separating the distributed human geometry from externally installed generation models and robot assets. Human-motion edits preserve frames outside a selected interval, while robot edits create immutable candidates whose reports govern acceptance and export. We evaluate server 0.5.1 and Gadget 0.15.2 with 156 core regression test executions, 49 Gadget executions, four CUDA generation/editing cases, a 30-frame G1 retargeting check, and a 3,600-frame synthetic G1 fixture paired with a suspended negative control. All four CUDA cases passed their numerical gates; the turning splice nevertheless retained a 14.3 cm support-foot drift proxy warning. The G1 positive fixture completed bounded simulation replay, whereas the suspended control was quarantined before replay. These results support selected integration and preservation contracts. They do not establish semantic-quality improvements, population-level feasibility, or hardware safety.
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Technical report on Kinora server 0.5.1 and Gadget 0.15.2. Code and release artifacts: this https URL

title: Martine: Benchmarking Multi-View 3D Surface Reconstruction Across Viewpoint Coverage, Resolution, and Lighting
summary: Controlled acquisition setups are widely used for high-accuracy multi-view 3D surface reconstruction, as they allow sensor configuration, image resolution, viewpoint distribution, and illumination to be specified. Yet benchmarking remains difficult, since reconstruction accuracy depends jointly on the reconstruction paradigm, object properties, and acquisition regime. Existing benchmarks often restrict viewpoint coverage, resolution, or illumination, which can bias comparisons towards methods suited to the chosen setting. Others lack accurate 3D ground truth or quantified image-to-geometry alignment, limiting their use for metric surface evaluation. We introduce Martine, a benchmark for controlled 3D object surface reconstruction. Martine comprises 28 objects, including transparent materials and fine structures, captured at 9568 x 6376 pixels from 84 views over a spherical cap under both single-light and multi-light regimes. It provides object-independent camera calibration, accurate 3D ground-truth scans, calibration and image-to-geometry accuracy quantified on test images, and 3D property masks for analysing errors by material properties, visibility, curvature and fine structures. Experiments across photogrammetry, classical multi-view stereo, neural implicit surfaces, Gaussian-splatting-based reconstruction, and multi-view photometric stereo show that Martine enables regime-aware evaluation with explicit control over reference-data accuracy. The benchmark resolves sub-millimetric reconstruction differences, with a best observed Chamfer distance of 0.058 mm over the evaluated visible surface.
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 23 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables. Project page: this https URL

title: Weight-Space Programming of Policies and Their Verification via Model Checking
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can write the weights of small neural networks directly, without gradient descent. This weight-space programming creates policies for sequential decision-making from a task description alone, but nothing guarantees that a written policy behaves as intended. We combine weight-space programming with probabilistic model checking. Given an environment modeled as a Markov decision process and a requirement in probabilistic computation tree logic (PCTL), an LLM writes all weights of a policy network, optionally repairs them on a dataset of optimal actions, and receives model-checking feedback until the requirement holds or a round limit is reached. The model checker Storm computes, rather than estimates from simulations, the probability that the policy satisfies the requirement, so every returned policy is verified. With two LLMs on three environments, the created policy of each of the 18 runs attains the optimal probability, before any dataset or model-checking feedback. Four of six policies programmed for two transporter jobs also complete three jobs with probability 1, so they generalize to a task that the LLM never saw. The pipeline also programs a policy that satisfies a complex safety requirement expressed with the PCTL until operator in all six runs. In one of them, dataset repair raised the accuracy to 98.4\% but broke the requirement, and one round of model-checking feedback restored it.

title: ScanDreamer: A Map-Grounded World Model for Quadrotor Navigation
summary: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at this https URL.
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to AICAP 2027; decision pending

title: Rethinking Geometric Depth in Monocular 3D Object Detection: A Projection-Consistent Reformulation
summary: Monocular 3D detection (Mono3D) hinges on recovering depth from a single image, for which the geometric formulation $z \approx f \cdot H / h_{2D}$ is widely adopted due to its simplicity and direct grounding in projective geometry. We show that this formulation harbors a systematic, projection-induced bias: substituting the 2D bounding-box height $h_{2D}$ recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation that persists even under ground-truth inputs. We address this front-surface bias with MonoPCA, a unified framework built on a projection-consistent reformulation. At its core, PCDepth retains the measurable $h_{2D}$ and closes the gap to center depth through an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, eliminating the bias without introducing ill-posed regression targets. Because PCDepth couples depth to predicted object size and orientation, attribute perception becomes essential. We therefore introduce GeoAlign, a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student, strengthening attribute perception at no inference cost. Across four challenging benchmarks, MonoPCA achieves SoTA performance, including a +1.44% AP$_{3D}$ gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D$_{OUT}$. Code is available at this https URL.

title: Building heterogeneous multistep workflows in automated microscopy: reward design and knowledge transfer for autonomous structure property discovery
summary: Autonomous microscopy can turn fast acquisition into scientific progress when it decides not only where to measure, but also what information to acquire, at what scan rate, and when to recalibrate the instrument. We develop a budget constrained framework for such multistep structure-property workflows. It combines explicit scientific rewards, action costs, instrument observation models, transfer of pre experiment knowledge into the online campaign, and evaluation kept independent of the controller. The transferred knowledge includes predictor accuracy and computational cost, empirical learner maturity functions that weight model-derived rewards, and drift characteristics established before controller training. Using a real electron energy-loss spectroscopy dataset, we run two complementary campaigns. In the first, the controller chooses between imaging and spectroscopy, image size, and scan speed. In the second, the instrument drifts and the controller also decides when to recalibrate. The campaigns show that response discovery and structure-property learning favor different surrogate models and acquisition strategies. They also show that simple acquisition rules form strong, practical baselines. Independent error analysis reveals where model uncertainty is and is not a reliable learning signal. In the drift campaign, explicit registration greatly improves positional accuracy, and the framework measures what this costs in spectroscopy throughput. Together, these results provide a reproducible way to design, compare, and audit autonomous experiments, and they define what microscopes must provide for deployment: independently executable actions, characterized scan and detector responses, timestamped registration telemetry, and complete action records.

title: Daily Emergency Call Volume Forecasting using Univariate and Multivariate TimeGPT
summary: This study investigates the potential of TimeGPT, a pretrained foundation model for timeseries, for forecasting daily emergency call volumes. Real-world emergency call data, comprising 2,101 daily observations, are used to evaluate both univariate and multivariate forecasting settings under one-step-ahead and seven-day multi-step-ahead scenarios. The multivariate forecasting incorporates temporal, meteorological, demographic, and socioeconomic variables. A chronological training, validation, and test split is adopted to prevent information leakage, while hyperparameters are selected using the validation set through grid search and early stopping when applicable. Forecasting performance is evaluated using multiple error metrics. Its forecasting performance is compared with several established forecasting approaches, including Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Regressors (SARIMAX), Poisson regression (PR), Negative Binomial regression (NBR), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). The results show that SARIMAX achieves the best overall performance in the univariate setting. In the multivariate setting, NBR and PR provide best performance. These findings indicate that the large-scale pretraining of TimeGPT do not necessarily translate into superior forecasting accuracy for emergency call volumes. Frugal methods trained solely on the available data remain better for this application.
comment: Keywords: Emergency calls; Prehospital emergency services; Time-series forecasting; Foundation models; TimeGPT; Univariate forecast; Multivariate forecast

title: ODSA: Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation
summary: Test-time scaling improves the accuracy of a language model's answers by spending more computation at inference time. Established methods do so either sequentially, revising a single solution over several passes, or in parallel, generating several independent solutions and selecting among them. We present ODSA (Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation), an LLM-directed scaling framework in which an orchestrator LLM is given existing test-time scaling methods as actions --- discovery of a new independent solution, comparison of existing solutions to build a better one, and acceptance of a proposed answer, which triggers its verification --- and directs stateless workers to carry them out. The orchestrator does not solve the problem itself: it allocates computation, feeds the results of earlier actions into later ones, and takes every action from a single context, so that each decision is informed by everything tried before. On Humanity's Last Exam, ODSA improves accuracy by 4.7 to 18.0 points across three models over a single direct call to the model with no test-time scaling. On LiveCodeBench, where a single direct call already solves most problems, it improves accuracy by 0.6 to 14.0 points.

title: GenISys: Integrated Ship Systems Design Using Subsystem-Conditional Tabular Diffussion
summary: Ship design requires coordinating coupled subsystems to satisfy engineering constraints and balance competing performance and cost objectives. Generative artificial intelligence has supported component design, but integrated ship generation must also account for interactions among hull geometry, structure, propulsion, and operation. This paper presents GenISys, a framework for generating integrated systems, demonstrated through early-stage bulk-carrier design. Its dataset contains 217,999 proposed designs, including 16,247 that satisfy the formulated engineering constraints. The proposed simultaneous conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (SCDDPM) generates subsystems together, allowing each subsystem model to respond to changes elsewhere during generation. Experiments compare this approach with monolithic whole-ship generation and sequential subsystem generation across five independent training runs per architecture. In a study targeting lower cost per tonne of cargo transported, designs were generated for a required voyage range of 5,000 nautical miles. SCDDPM produced designs satisfying the formulated engineering constraints and meeting a common low-cost target in 55.70% of generation requests, compared with 51.10% for the monolithic model and 47.54% for the sequential model. These correspond to 9.0% and 17.2% more qualifying designs, respectively, while maintaining similar estimated transport costs. These results show how generative artificial intelligence can coordinate subsystems to generate feasible, high-performing integrated systems.

title: Perturbation Profiles of Scanpath Classifiers: What Reading, Code-Comprehension and Video Decoders Are Sensitive To
summary: When a scanpath descriptor discriminates a task, it is rarely clear what the discrimination rests on. We propose a perturbation profile for trial-level descriptors. Five transformations each destroy one stated property while preserving a listed set of invariants: fixation order, duration-position coupling, the duration distribution, orientation and handedness, and fine spatial structure. The classifier is refit, and the drop in participant-held-out AUC is the pipeline's sensitivity to that property. Because refitting lets the learner use redundant information, this describes the refitted pipeline, not what a fitted classifier used. Intervals come from a participant bootstrap that refits; in simulations at the sample sizes analysed, where the target was zero they excluded zero at a pooled rate of at most 2.5%, and they covered the target in 99.6% of 2720 cases. We profiled seven descriptors on twelve binary problems from three public datasets: reading (SB-SAT, 95 participants), program comprehension (EMIP, up to 159) and video and game viewing (GazeBase, 60). Permuting fixation order raised the AUC of a descriptor built on mean saccade amplitude on three problems (by up to 0.23), because permutation turns amplitude into a measure of spatial spread. A "comprehension" contrast that pooled two programs reached AUC 0.70 with a spread-only baseline and fell to 0.47 within one program: the profile located the confound in stimulus layout. On native versus non-native readers, recurrence was sensitive to order and to jitter at the scale of text lines but not of characters, while a two-feature duration and amplitude descriptor reached the same AUC (0.65). A graph descriptor built on the code's tokens was the strongest non-baseline descriptor on the program contrast (0.78; 0.87 with boosted trees). The interpreted results held under longer runs and three seeds; under a second learner 15 of 16 kept t

title: An Interpretable Fuzzy Tree for Turbofan Remaining Useful Life with an Auditable Per-Component Diagnostic Layer
summary: Data-driven remaining useful life (RUL) estimators for turbofan engines are accurate but opaque, and their internal features typically encode remaining life rather than any specific component's state. This paper presents an interpretable genetic fuzzy tree that predicts RUL from cruise-condition sensor means on N-CMAPSS while exposing a per-component diagnostic layer inspectable rule by rule. The tree follows the engine hierarchy: sensors to component health, then to bounded component damage, spool damage, and RUL, so each level answers a different maintenance question. Training is staged so the prognostic objective cannot reshape the diagnostic layers: health leaves are fitted to physical targets and frozen, a deterministic fuzzy damage map with fleet-referenced thresholds is imposed on each component, and only the aggregation is optimized for RUL. It consumes 13 cruise-mean scalars per cycle rather than a trajectory, which removes any sequence model. On the native split it reaches 8.44 cycles RMSE on the multi-fault subset and 11.51 across all modes with 333 free parameters, 411 total rules, 32 to 12,000 times fewer than compiled baselines. An exhaustive sensor search bounds which components are diagnosable under the tested cruise-mean design, and the rule base is structured to admit formal verification, which this study does not discharge.

title: Feel My Focus: Gaze-Triggered Digital Twin Creation for Remote Collaboration
summary: We present Feel My Focus, a gaze-triggered mixed reality (MR) demonstration that enables rapid creation and sharing of lightweight 3D digital twins during remote collaboration. Unlike systems that use gaze primarily as a referential pointer, Feel My Focus treats sustained visual attention as a generative action: a fixation on a physical object initiates single-image capture, attention-guided segmentation, and one-shot 3D reconstruction, allowing a remote partner to inspect and discuss the object in situ. The system integrates gaze-tracking glasses, modular segmentation and reconstruction services, and an MR client for runtime streaming and interaction. This design prioritizes responsiveness and experiential continuity over photometric fidelity. We report observations from a public demonstration, highlighting design trade-offs, failure modes, and user control considerations for deploying gaze-triggered generative systems in real-world collaborative settings.

title: MICE: Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder - A Hierarchical Foundation Model for Mouse Behavior
summary: Quantifying mouse behavior from pose is a foundational tool in neuroscience, ethology, drug discovery, and animal welfare. Self-supervised foundation models are a natural fit, but a foundation model for mouse behavior must handle social behavior - many behaviors that matter (aggression, courtship, mounting, allogrooming) are inherently multi-animal. Existing self-supervised pose models fall short: they encode each animal independently and discard interaction signal, hard-code the animal count, and pretrain one dataset at a time. We introduce MICE (Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder), a hierarchical foundation model for mouse behavior that pretrains jointly on six mouse-pose corpora spanning one to four mice and 7 to 27 keypoints. MICE combines a hierarchical individual encoder capturing per-mouse kinematics at multiple temporal scales with a Perceiver-style social encoder whose learned latent codebook decouples parameter count from animal count, so a single checkpoint serves any group size without retraining. Across four evaluation protocols spanning six datasets, MICE matches or exceeds prior keypoint-based baselines, and layer-wise probing shows the social stage incrementally improves discriminability beyond the individual encoder. Code, weights, and data are available at this https URL.
comment: NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). 25 pages, 4 figures. Code: this https URL

title: ColNav: Uncertainty-Aware Spacetime Collision Checking with Bounding Volume Hierarchies
summary: Safe navigation for mobile robots in dynamic and uncertain environments requires planning paths that avoid collisions with other moving targets. Typically this involves forward propagating the robot motion and checking for collisions at sampled points in space and time. Such methods can miss collisions between sampled points and are not robust to uncertainty in the state estimates. We propose ColNav, a robust collision check formulation with geometric volumes. The key aspect of our approach is encoding the uncertainty in the targets' and the ego robot's positions and velocities into spacetime tubes, in two variants that consume bounded-set and Gaussian uncertainty descriptions, respectively. The tubes are organised in bounding volume hierarchies, so that a single tree traversal covers the entire horizon, rather than testing sampled time instants, and returns a robust geometric certificate together with an estimate of the time to collision. Static and dynamic obstacles share the same representation. Our approach reaches the goal with a 100% success rate under prediction model mismatch, where the best baseline reaches 65%, and maintains up to three times the clearance in dense traffic. We also validate real-time operation on a physical robot.

title: PA-SaR: Perception-Aware Learning, Control, and Coordination for Multi-Robot Search and Rescue
summary: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.

title: A Trust Region Approach for Learning Schrödinger Bridges
summary: We study the numerical approximation of Schrödinger Bridges in the setting where samples from the target distribution are unavailable and only an unnormalized target density is given. In this regime, the widely used iterative proportional fitting (IPF) procedure (and its variants) often exhibits severe numerical instabilities, stemming from ill-conditioned underlying control problems and from the fact that the optimal solution may lie far from the initialization. To address these issues, we propose a trust region variant of IPF that constrains successive updates to remain at a fixed Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current iterate. This restriction significantly improves numerical stability. Moreover, we show that the resulting method admits an interpretation as a mirror descent scheme with an adaptively chosen step size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging sampling tasks.
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026; Takeshi Koshizuka and Lorenz Richter contributed equally

title: FlowEval: How Much Adaptation Does an Embodied Foundation Model Need at Deployment?
summary: Large-scale pretraining is reducing the amount of adaptation required to deploy embodied foundation models, but it is not guaranteed that a pretrained model already provide the level of performance required in every deployment. Practitioners therefore need to understand how well a pretrained model matches a target deployment and how much adaptation data is left to be collected. We study whether a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations can reveal whether and how much target-domain data will be required before any adaptation. We introduce FlowEval, a set of training-free metrics that use the flow-matching objective to probe an embodied foundation model with a set of demonstrations. FlowEval quantifies predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations to assess how well a pretrained model fits a target deployment. Across four embodied foundation model families: Pi-0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T, and DreamZero, FlowEval distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across real-world and simulated manipulation. Further, by finetuning Pi-0.5 and GR00T on 17 RoboCasa365 manipulation tasks, we showed that FlowEval correlates with how success rate improves as additional adaptation data is provided. Together, these results suggest that FlowEval can serve as a lightweight, training-free diagnostic of how much model--deployment adaptation may be required.

title: Optimizing Multi-Tier Intermediation in Programmatic Advertising: A DAG-Based Mechanism for Supply Path Optimization
summary: Digital programmatic advertising operates through complex, multi-hop supply chains. The opacity of these intermediary networks leads to significant efficiency losses, often referred to as the ``ad-tech tax.'' While current industry practices utilize heuristic Supply Path Optimization (SPO) to trim inefficient routes, they fail to optimize the equilibrium of the entire network. This paper extends previous work on Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) intermediation models by applying them to traceable programmatic supply chains mapped via the OpenRTB SupplyChain object. We introduce multi-attribute utility functions and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) to account for substitutable routing (OR nodes) and percentage-based fee structures. Furthermore, we outline a computational methodology and experimental framework using public \texttt{schain} and \texttt{this http URL} data to benchmark optimal Nash social welfare against current uncoordinated market outcomes.

title: Means vs. Foundation Models for Emergency Call Forecasting
summary: This study investigates whether generalized means can achieve forecasting performance comparable to that of TimeGPT for daily emergency call volume prediction. Specifically, two families of generalized means, the Hölder means (HM) and the Lehmer means (LM), are evaluated against fine-tuned TimeGPT across forecasting horizons ranging from one to seven days. Forecasting performance is assessed on a real-world emergency call dataset using multiple error metrics, and Diebold-Mariano test. Experimental results show that HM and LM achieve nearly identical predictive performance across all forecasting horizons. For short-term forecasting, both generalized means outperform TimeGPT, with reductions of mean absolute error (MAE) approximately 1.24\% and 2.48\% at horizons of one and three days, respectively. Conversely, TimeGPT achieves a lower error at the seven-day horizon, with an descresing of MAE by 1.98\%. However, Diebold-Mariano tests reveal no statistically significant differences between the methods at the evaluated horizons. These findings suggest that generalized means can provide competitive forecasting performance compared with a energyvore foundation model.
comment: Keywords: Prehospital emergency calls; Foundation models; TimeGPT; Hölder means; Lehmer means

title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents
summary: We built a hybrid multi-agent trading system that combines large language model (LLM) analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves. We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.
comment: 37 pages, including appendices. Code and supporting materials available upon request

title: Measuring Generative AI Content in Political Campaigns: Evidence of Rising Adoption and Non-Disclosure
summary: The use of generative AI in political campaigns has drawn public concern and policy attention. Public concerns range from distrust of candidates to skepticism about the authenticity and accuracy of political advertising, including AI-generated images and video. Nearly half of U.S. states have enacted laws that prohibit, or require disclosure of, "materially deceptive" AI-generated content (AIGC) in elections to guard against these concerns. This study measures how candidates and their campaigns produce and circulate AIGC during an election cycle. We develop two measures that estimate not only wether campaigns use AIGC, but how much they produce (magnitude) and in what forms (modality). We apply these measures to a novel dataset of text and images from the campaign websites, X accounts, and emails of 12,977 candidates for U.S. political office from 2023 to 2025. We report three findings. First, detectable AIGC from campaigns increased significantly across modalities over the observation window, and campaigns that use AIGC frequently do not disclose it. Second, incumbents' campaigns produced significantly less AIGC than challengers' campaigns. Third, candidates in states with AIGC disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less AIGC than candidates in other states. Our method and findings have implications for transparency and trust in elections, and on state laws that regulate AI use in campaigns. Because current state laws largely target mainly "materially deceptive" content, we identify additional policy mechanisms that could increase electoral transparency and improve trust as AIGC becomes more prevalent.

title: RADE: Risk-Adjusted Deployment Efficiency, A Framework for Routing, Memory, and Escalation in Safe LLM Systems
summary: A deployed language model does not merely answer questions. It spends computation, consumes time, consults evidence, exposes memory, invites or avoids human review, and sometimes makes mistakes whose consequences are radically unequal. Yet LLM systems are still commonly compared as if the relevant object were a single model and the relevant outcome were a single benchmark score. This paper argues that the unit of analysis should instead be the deployment policy: the mechanism that decides when to retrieve, when to remember, when to call a larger model, when to verify, and when not to answer at all. We introduce risk-adjusted deployment efficiency (RADE), a system-level objective that scores the utility a deployment delivers net of inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected failure cost, while treating harms that cannot be priced as hard budgets alongside constraints on latency, privacy, and resources. The framework brings selective routing, retrieval and governed memory, efficient specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and human escalation into a common account. We then examine five deployment regimes in which the same nominal LLM capability leads to different rational architectures, and propose a reporting protocol based on risk-coverage behavior, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load. The central claim is modest but consequential: frontier capability should be treated as a resource to allocate, not a default state to maintain. A safe and sustainable system is not the one that always uses the strongest model; it is the one that spends capability where the reduction in risk or increase in utility justifies the cost.

title: Enhancing Balance and Posture in Material Handling Tasks with a Wearable Robotic Tail
summary: Frequent heavy lifting is linked to musculoskeletal strain, with lower back pain affecting up to 40% of manual labourers. Inspired by animals using tails for balance, we developed a wearable robotic tail as a dynamic counterbalance. Ten participants performed an imitated shelf loading/unloading task across three conditions: active tail, passive tail, and no tail. Kinematics, centre of pressure, and muscle activation (gastrocnemius, erector spinae, tibialis anterior, biceps brachii) were measured. Compared with no tail, the active tail achieved >20 mm reduction in centre of pressure peak displacement, 4.3 degree reduction in trunk motion, and >9% and >20% reductions in erector spinae and gastrocnemius activity, respectively. The passive tail produced smaller reductions, suggesting passive counterbalancing helps while active movement augments it further. Biceps brachii activation increased with the active versus passive tail. The ankle kinematics and tibialis anterior activation were unchanged. These findings support wearable robotic tails for improving balance during material handling.

title: HINT-VLM: Humanoid Interactive Navigation over Rough Terrain with Embodiment-Grounded Vision-Language Model
summary: Humanoid robots have achieved significant progress in locomotion and manipulation, enabling traversal over rough terrain and richer interaction with the environment, such as moving obstacles. However, most traditional navigation methods assume non-interactive environments and focus only on traversal. While Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) approaches relax this assumption, prior efforts have largely focused on flat environments and reactive interaction, rather than predicting object movability and planning ahead. These limitations become critical in outdoor rough-terrain scenarios, where robots must jointly reason about terrain traversability and object movability. In this work, we address NAMO for humanoid robots in cluttered outdoor rough terrain by proposing a hybrid planning framework that combines semantic priors from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) with embodied robot interaction data through a Gaussian process (GP) residual model. The GP corrects the VLM-derived movability prior to produce embodiment-grounded probabilistic movability estimates, which are then incorporated into hierarchical uncertainty-aware planning. The proposed approach allows humanoids to jointly leverage locomotion and manipulation for efficient and safe navigation, representing the first solution to NAMO in rough terrain through predictive movability reasoning and probabilistic VLM integration.

title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization
summary: We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

title: Brain-Aligned Latent Actions: Imposing Premotor Cortex Geometry on a Robot's Action Vocabulary
summary: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Robot manipulation results (CALVIN) will be added in a later version

title: Query- and Candidate-Aware Long User Sequence Modeling for Sponsored Product Ranking in Search
summary: User sequence modeling is widely used in recommendation and advertising. Search ranking presents an additional challenge: the current query expresses immediate intent, while a candidate product determines which parts of a user's long-term history are relevant. We present a production sequence framework for sponsored-product ranking that augments recent behavior with two retrieval channels over long-term history: candidate-nearest-neighbor retrieval and query-nearest-neighbor retrieval. The selected actions are encoded together with dedicated query and candidate context tokens, while candidate-aware early fusion injects the candidate into every history token. Offline ablations show that dual retrieval improves major ranking metrics relative to the production baseline. In an online A/B test on sponsored-product search traffic, the model increased CTR, attributed conversion rate, and orders per impression.
comment: Accepted to ACM RecSys 2026 Workshop on Context-Aware Recommender Systems (CARS)

title: SurfScaff3D: Bridging Geometric and Semantic Representations for LLM-based 3D Object Generation
summary: Creating high-quality 3D content has traditionally required specialist expertise and experience with complex tools. The growing ecosystem of AI-assisted creativity demands accessible and intuitive 3D generation systems. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising directions, yet extending their generative capabilities to 3D remains fundamentally challenging because existing 3D representations are not naturally compatible with language-based reasoning. Current approaches either depend on expensive fine-tuning or impose restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes. We argue that the mismatch between LLM-native reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations is a core bottleneck of LLM-driven 3D generation. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning. Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D, an interactive framework for text and image-to-3D generation. HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. Its hierarchical part-level semantic labels enable targeted, natural-language edits at any level of granularity without re-running generation. Further, HPS offers explicit per-patch control over surface detail, enabling more expressive geometry capable of representing arbitrary objects. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.

title: The Average Patient: Do Simulated Psychiatric Patients Answer Like Real People?
summary: Language models are used as simulated psychiatric patients to train clinicians and evaluate AI therapists, and are judged by plausibility or total scores. We give a framework for simulated respondents: an information budget bounds how much simulated patients can differ, and an average-patient hypothesis, that a model answers each item at the level typical of the named condition and severity, implies little variation, a full profile of the condition's typical symptoms and totals at or above the top of the stated severity band. We examine these implications at matched totals on item-level data from eight human samples, including a clinical and an instructed-feigning sample. Across 17 models, simulated patients vary 1.5 to 11 times less than real respondents with the same total and on most questionnaires endorse nearly every symptom at a middling level; on the PHQ-9 their symptoms covary less like real ones. People, honest or feigning, answer "not at all" about as often as genuine patients with the same totals, and more often than every model. Single answers are highly concentrated, and prompt changes, published personas, larger models and reasoning reduce the pattern without removing it. In interviews, patients told a severity are rated as having nearly every symptom, so an assessment agent's recognition of absent symptoms goes untested, and scored against the stated severity the agent places a quarter of them in their band, against about half of patients given a real symptom profile. Having the model word such a profile restores half to two thirds of the variation.

title: A Theoretical Reduction From Membership Inference to Reconstruction Attacks Against Learners
summary: We study reconstruction attacks, which recover training data from a learned model. In our adversarial model, the adversary designs a hard instance, drawn from a parameterized family of data distributions, and is given the parameter used to generate it. Our main contribution is a general reduction showing that, in this model, membership inference (determining whether a given datapoint was used for training) implies reconstruction: for a training set of size $n$, a membership test with recall at least $q(n)$ and false-positive rate $O(\delta^2/n^2)$ yields a reconstruction algorithm that, with probability $1 - O(\delta)$, outputs only training points, and recovers $\Omega(n \cdot q(n))$ of them in expectation. This reduction applies to any learning algorithm. For stochastic convex optimization (SCO), we make the reduction computationally efficient over exponentially large domains via structured distributions whose support is partitioned into polynomially many categories of exponentially many elements each, so that reconstruction iterates over categories rather than the full support. Combining this with an existing membership inference result for SCO, we prove that any learning algorithm achieving low excess risk over all distributions admits a polynomial-time reconstruction attack recovering $\Omega(n)$ training points, even when the underlying distribution has exponentially large support.

title: A Sequential Monte Carlo Method for Data Assimilation in Subsurface Flow Systems with Hierarchical Uncertainty
summary: Subsurface flow systems often involve hierarchical geological uncertainty, meaning both higher-level metaparameters and cell-by-cell properties are uncertain. This leads to challenges for data assimilation because both sets of parameters must be estimated. In this work we develop an adaptive-tempered sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) procedure for joint Bayesian estimation of these quantities. The method uses noncentered geological parameterizations, with geomodel realizations represented by metaparameters and Gaussian latent variables that are independent under the prior. Adaptive likelihood tempering, importance weighting, resampling, and blockwise Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) mutation are applied at each iteration. Flow surrogates are used for all function evaluations. The hierarchical SMC procedure is further extended to treat successive data assimilation. In this case, existing posterior particles are updated in a manner that accounts for correlations in surrogate model errors across observation batches. We consider two distinct 3D systems with hierarchical uncertainty. The first is a faulted carbon storage system containing three stacked aquifers and two extensive faults. Principal component analysis is used to represent target-aquifer heterogeneity, while geological metaparameters characterize uncertain aquifer and fault properties. The second is a channelized oil-water system containing three facies with uncertain properties. A latent diffusion model represents variability in channel geometry and facies realizations. For the four synthetic true models considered, SMC posterior metaparameter distributions and flow predictions agree closely with reference MCMC results. SMC, however, requires fewer function evaluations and provides speedups of 2.5--7.0 for single-stage data assimilation. Even greater speedups are achieved with multiple GPUs.

title: Self-Indexing Latent Memories for Access-Aware Continual Instruction Tuning of LLMs
summary: Continual instruction tuning often preserves old skills with task-private modules. Inference still requires selecting the right module from the prompt alone. We introduce Task-Isolated Latent Adapter Continual Training (TILA-CT), a replay-free method that makes each task module self-indexing. Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation, the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context. For access, its persistent state provides the routing prototype used by a shared prompt-only router. On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score, with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 acquisition and 64.17 final macro score. Across 6 backbones, final scores remain within 1.5 points of acquisition. Ablations support memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9\%, and oracle routing recovers 1.21 final macro points. These results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it.

title: Streaming Failure Forecasting: VLA Failure Monitors That Keep Learning After Deployment
summary: Failure monitors for vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained offline and then frozen. After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras drift, and the policy itself is updated or moved to new tasks. On recorded real-robot runs, after a switch of task or policy version, a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance. We present Streaming Failure Forecasting (SFF), a monitor that keeps learning from the one label every episode provides: whether it succeeded. SFF keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last linear layer after each episode, at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core. Its alarm threshold moves only after successes, which in simulation kept false alarms near target except when two drifts came at once. With every setting locked before testing, SFF ranks failures better than the same monitor kept frozen on 4 of 5 simulated test suites under unannounced drift, and above resetting on detected drift on every suite. Carried with its locked learner settings to 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced switches of task or policy version, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch. A deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen: refitting its readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes we tested.
comment: 25 pages, 13 figures, 9 tables. A short version was accepted at the Sim2Real2Field and EEAI workshops at CoRL 2026. Project page: this https URL

title: A Physical Testbed for Self-Driving Laboratories: Comparing Bayesian and Agentic Optimization in a Minimal Closed-Loop Color Formulation Task
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate laboratory robotics and automation with AI-driven decision-making to close the design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycle. However, physical testbeds that combine off-the-shelf hardware and AI into a functioning closed-loop workflow remain in early stages of development, and their integration with commercial laboratory automation is comparatively less developed. In this work, we develop a physical testbed that assembles and integrates commercially available laboratory automation instruments and demonstrate continuous, closed-loop, autonomous operation over 24 cumulative hours of unattended experimentation. We validate this platform on a minimal closed-loop discovery task in which the system autonomously formulates aqueous dye mixtures to match a target absorbance spectrum. The system completed six independent campaigns, each consisting of 48 closed-loop iterations over approximately four hours. In every campaign, the system autonomously selected, dispensed, and measured each mixture, with an AI-driven decision-making algorithm determining subsequent formulations without human intervention. Using this testbed, we compared the performance of two AI-driven decision-making algorithms, traditional Bayesian optimization (BO) and an agentic approach, in selecting mixtures under a fixed total-volume constraint. The agentic optimizer matched target absorbance spectra using fewer iterations than BO, with reductions up to 52%, and converged on a solution for one target that BO failed to match within 48 iterations. These results demonstrate a reference physical platform for SDLs that can evaluate both established and emerging AI strategies, including large language model (LLM)-directed optimization, before their deployment in real-world applications where experiments may be costly and time-consuming to prepare.

title: Resolvent Ellipsoid for Minty Set Inclusions
summary: We study Minty set inclusion on a compact convex set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ with a set-valued operator $A : \mathcal{X} \rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}^d$. Under the Minty promise, the goal is to compute $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $u \in A(x)$ such that $\sup_{y \in \mathcal{X}} \langle u, x - y \rangle \le \varepsilon$. Our approach is geometric and we work in the fixed-scale constrained-resolvent oracle model, where a query at anchor $a$ is assumed to return a resolvent point $x^+$ together with the Yosida vector $g_{\eta}(a) = (a - x^+)/\eta$. We prove that each oracle response yields a sharp dichotomy: either the returned point provides an $\varepsilon$-SVI certificate, or the Yosida vector defines a strict separating normal for the Minty set. Thus, a single black-box resolvent query supplies either a certified candidate solution or a valid geometric cut. Combining this separation principle with the ellipsoid method, we obtain RESOLVENT-ELLIPSOID, an algorithm that computes an $\varepsilon$-SVI in $\mathcal{O}\!\left(\operatorname{poly}(d, \log(1/\varepsilon))\right)$ black-box oracle calls to the fixed-scale constrained resolvent. For monotone inclusions, our algorithm gives, to our knowledge, the first $\mathcal{O}\!\left(\mathrm{poly}(d, \log(1/\varepsilon))\right)$ black-box guarantee in the fixed-scale resolvent model.
comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026

title: LocateAnyMesh: Grounding 3D Mesh Queries in 2D Images with Vision-Language Models
summary: Textured 3D meshes specify object geometry and appearance, making them a natural query for finding a particular asset in an image. We introduce LocateAnyMesh, a vision-language model that uses the mesh itself as part of its prompt. A frozen 3D encoder maps colored surface points to a compact token sequence, which a learned connector places alongside image and instruction tokens. We evaluate two grounding models with PPAT mesh tokens: LAM-Select selects image-region proposals, while LAM-Direct predicts coordinates directly. Neither requires rendered query views or view-template matching. New objects require a single encoder pass and no object-specific fine-tuning. LAM-Select improves localization on the reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation. Secondary experiments compare mesh encoders, and a LAM-Direct study isolates surface color. A single-seed LAM-Select continuation supplies pointing and mesh-only description evidence without replacing the reported localization model. The results support mesh tokens as a query representation, with remaining limitations in presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.

title: Homological Barriers to Stable Learning of First-Order Nash Equilibria
summary: We identify a homological barrier to stable learning of local Nash equilibria, also known as first-order Nash equilibria (FONE), in constrained non-concave differentiable games. We consider continuous deterministic learning dynamics that fix every FONE point and aim to attract all initial conditions to the full FONE set. We show that this convergence guarantee is impossible when the target set has nontrivial positive-degree cohomology, such as that arising from a loop, and the state space is compact and contractible. We exhibit this barrier in a simple non-concave quadratic zero-sum game on a box whose exact FONE set consists of a diagonal six-edge loop and an isolated point. Consequently, no such dynamics can make the full FONE set a stable global attractor. We further show that degree two is the minimal polynomial degree at which this barrier can arise and extend the construction to obtain nontrivial homology in arbitrarily high degrees. Finally, we establish that the barrier persists for sufficiently small approximate-FONE targets under small perturbations, yielding an open, positive-volume family of quadratic zero-sum games with the same homological barrier.
comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026

title: Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation
summary: Compression can preserve a language model's average accuracy while selectively degrading individual capabilities. Whether these losses follow method-specific patterns or a transferable order is unclear. We applied seven perturbation and compression methods to eight instruction-tuned models, scoring 16 tasks in four answer formats against preregistered predictions. Short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order under four random perturbations with different mechanisms (median correlation 0.90) and, within each model, under pruning and quantization (0.875). Intact answer margin, answer frequency and answer format predicted this order. Fragility profiles measured under random perturbation predicted which tasks and facts compression removes first and, after four-task calibration, held-out task accuracy (median absolute error 0.11-0.12, against 0.20-0.21 for uniform decline); profiles borrowed from other model families did almost as well. The order did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization or hold for long-form tasks. Within short answers, what compression removes is predictable before deployment.

title: Direct GPU Energy Measurements of Batch-Level Sharing in Mixture-of-Experts and Recurrent Models
summary: Energy claims for efficient neural networks are often inferred from operation counts. We report direct GPU energy measurements on two workloads that batch very differently, recurrent policies in GPU-vectorised multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, and ask one question of both: can the rows of a batch be made to share computation, across the batch and over time, at a measured saving? On recurrent policies the answer so far is no. Shared activity patterns exist but rarely last one step, masking a frozen policy fails, and trained-in masks succeed only because a fixed mask is equivalent to a narrow GRU, at 11x the energy of a small dense policy in our implementation. Test-time steering adds nothing beyond re-picking on either workload. On MoE models the answer is yes, and granularity decides how much: on Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware routing reads 25-31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05, with benchmark changes within noise at 500 items, and uses 12-18% less energy per token on a fused forward. We also introduce persistence-aware OEA, a one-parameter rule that keeps the batch-aware cut with about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch 32-64, though its energy has not yet been measured. These are pilot measurements on one GPU type, and we state their limits.

title: SurgTAP-3D: A Large-Scale Cross-Surgery Video Dataset with Contact-Aware 3D Motion Tracking
summary: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO)

title: Compute Regeneration through Re-Productization: Reorganizing Retired Edge AI Silicon into a Delivered Multilingual Service Robot
summary: Useful edge hardware can lose product support while retaining substantial computation. We treat this as systems design: compute regeneration here means re-productization, retaining the compute module while redesigning the surrounding product organization. Our case is GEdgeBot, a multilingual service robot built around a retired 32 GB Jetson AGX Xavier. A source-grounded inventory shows the box alone supplies inference, while the combined system exposes five on-device AI services, a seven-language speech chain, three sensing domains, and one deterministic seven-byte control boundary. AI and orchestration stay on the Xavier; finite motor-pulse generation on an STM32F407. Audits cover the six-mode control state machine, readiness barriers and sound orientation. Historical single-prototype measurements report 1,782 MB GPU memory with YOLO, Whisper-small, and NLLB-200 resident, a direct-control p99 deviation rising from 0.24 to 49.93 ms under concurrent AI load, and six of six trigger-to-follow demonstrations at 4.35 s mean latency, with conversational voice unavailable. A November campaign restores an isolated inference stack, re-measures AI workloads, and repeats control-frame runs. Driving two execution organisations with the same 6,000 measured 50 ms frame intervals shows the finite-pulse boundary removes host jitter from the pulse train but not the command start phase; its stopping bound is host-enforced, while the MCU 16-bit pulse field is unclamped. A six-check static audit exposes a host--MCU queue mismatch, and a 14-scenario replay executes the audited main() dispatcher across six modes with zero physical device opens and 54 contract-checked frames. Results support an existence claim and a reproducible architectural hypothesis, not fleet-level reliability. The 208 direct-control ratio remains unreplicated; MCU waveform capture and on-site fault injection remain open.

title: Scalable Counterfactual Explanations for Time Series via Policy Learning
summary: Generating counterfactual (CF) explanations for time series is challenging due to complex temporal dependencies and the computational inefficiency of traditional instance-specific optimization. We propose a policy learning framework for counterfactual explanation in time series, trained as a one-step contextual-bandit policy-learning problem. By training an actor-critic agent in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder, our method learns a transferable policy that captures global structural regularities. Unlike existing methods that rely on iterative optimization for each new input, the learned policy enables direct generation of valid and plausible counterfactuals through a single forward pass, avoiding per-instance optimization at inference time. Experiments on 13 UCR benchmark datasets show that our framework achieves high validity and strong plausibility across multiple anomaly detection metrics. Overall, by decoupling counterfactual generation from per-instance optimization, the proposed method provides an efficient and scalable alternative to existing approaches for time series counterfactual explanations.

title: Data-Driven Precision Control of Soft Helicoid Robots
summary: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.
comment: Submitted to npj Robotics. 44 pages, supplementary information included

title: CASCoDe: A Closed-Loop Agentic Framework for Analog Sizing and Layout Co-Design
